title: Dirty but Clean Rivers

paragraphs.text: Fire and flood are two of humanity’s worst nightmares, so people have always sought to control them. Forest fires are snuffed out as quickly as possible and the flow of rivers is regulated by weirs and dams. At least, that is how it used to be. Over time, foresters have learned that forests need fires to clear out the brush and even to get seeds to germinate, and a similar revelation is now dawning on hydrologists. Rivers — and the ecosystems they support — need floods too.

Scientists have been investigating this hypothesis on the Colorado River, which runs through the Grand Canyon in the USA. Floods once raged down the river every year, creating the Grand Canyon landscape. Each spring the snow would melt and swell the Colorado River to a flow of around 1,500 cubic meters a second, and every eight years or so, that figure rose to almost 3,500 cubic meters. These floods infused the river with sediment and sand, carved its beaches and built its sandbars.

However, since 1963 when the Glen Canyon Dam was built just upstream of the Grand Canyon, observers have noticed a gradual decline in the size and number of sandbars. Because most of the sand that was carried yearly to the Grand Canyon by the Colorado River now gets trapped behind the dam, many fear that the sandbars will gradually erode away and never be replaced. Nowadays, the only sediment that the river collects comes from tiny, undammed tributaries. Even this is not much use as these tributaries are not powerful enough to distribute the sediment in an ecologically valuable way.

This lack of flooding has harmed local wildlife. The humpback chub, for example, a small native fish of the Colorado River, thrived in the rust-red waters. Recently, though, its population has crashed. At first sight, it looked as if the reason was that the chub were being eaten by trout introduced for sport fishing in the mid-twentieth century. But trout and chub co-existed until the Glen Canyon Dam was built, so something else is going on.

Steve Gloss, of the United States Geological Survey (USGS), reckons that the chub’s decline is the result of their losing their most valuable natural defence, the Colorado’s rusty sediment. This sediment is what creates the river’s famous red water is the reason it was given the name ‘colorado,’ as it means ‘colored red’ in Spanish. The chub were well adapted to the poor visibility created by this thick, red water and depended on it to hide from predators. Without the cloudy water, the chub became vulnerable.

And the chub are not alone. In the years since the Glen Canyon Dam was built, some species, such as the razorback sucker, have vanished altogether. Meanwhile, the common carp, which would have been hard put to survive in the savage waters of the undammed canyon, have moved in.

In an attempt to restore some of the pre-dam river conditions, controlled flooding of the Colorado River by releases from Glen Canyon Dam was proposed as a way to manage sediment and sand in the Grand Canyon. The floods were expected to suspend the sand deposited on the river bottom by lower flows and move it along the riverbanks where it would be above water after the flood receded. In this way, the limited sand resources could be utilized to preserve habitat for plants and animals and used by visitors to the area.

Controlled flooding may have seemed the obvious answer, but it is easier said than done. Floods were sent down the Grand Canyon in 1996 and 2004, and the results were mixed. In 1996, the flood was allowed to go on too long. To start with, all seemed well. The floodwaters built up sandbars and infused the river with sediment. Eventually, however, the continued flow washed most of the sediment out of the canyon. This problem was avoided in 2004, but unfortunately, on that occasion, the volume of sand behind the dam was too low to rebuild the sandbars.

For future controlled floods, scientists have recommended that the USGS wait until the volume of sediment is three times greater than it was in 2004. Even so, it may turn out to be an empty gesture. At less than 1,200 cubic meters a second, such a flood would be smaller than even an average spring flood, let alone one of the mightier deluges of the past. Those great floods moved massive quantities of sediment through the Grand Canyon, making a muddy mess of silt and muck and, in fact, doing nature’s work.
